name: Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary
tagline: Guras forest on the Singalila Range, a 4 km walk from Hilley
meta_description: Barsey (Varsey) Rhododendron Sanctuary guide: the 4 km Hilley walk, Guras Kunj hut, bloom dates, birds, entry fees, Okhrey stays and how to get there.
summary: Barsey, officially Varsey, Rhododendron Sanctuary covers about 104 km² of the Singalila Range where Sikkim meets Nepal and West Bengal. Most people walk 4 km, 1.5–2 hours, from Hilley to the Guras Kunj hut at about 3,000 m. Come mid-March to April for rhododendron bloom, or October to December for clear Kangchenjunga views.
intro: Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, spelt Varsey on official records and Wikipedia, protects about 104 km² of forest on the Singalila Range in the south-west corner of Sikkim. Nepal lies to the west and West Bengal to the south, across the Rambong Khola stream. The forests are thick with rhododendron, which people here call guras in Nepali, along with oak, magnolia and fir. In spring the slopes flower in red, pink and white.

The sanctuary has three entry points: Hilley, Dentam and Soreng. Hilley is by far the most used, because it is reachable by road and the walk from there to Barsey is only about 4 km. The trail is wide and gently graded, 1.5–2 hours up, and ends at the Guras Kunj trekkers' hut on an open ridge at about 3,000 m. On clear mornings you see Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Pandim to the north.

Most visitors sleep in Okhrey, about 30 minutes below Hilley, and walk in and out in a day. Others stay a night in the simple hut for sunset and sunrise. For a budget trip it costs little: a shared jeep to Okhrey, a homestay, a car to Hilley and the entry fee. Rhododendrons bloom from March to May, with the usual peak from mid-March to April. October to December is best for views.

story.title: Guras on the Singalila Range
paras: Guras is the Nepali word for rhododendron, and in this corner of Sikkim it is the tree that marks the seasons. Rhododendron arboreum, the tree rhododendron with deep red flowers, is the national flower of Nepal, whose border runs along the ridge above Barsey. Sikkim chose another species, Rhododendron niveum, as its state tree. Several species grow in the sanctuary at different heights, which is why the flowering moves uphill through March, April and May.

The plants were famous long before the sanctuary existed. In 1848–49 the botanist Joseph Hooker travelled through Sikkim, much of it with Archibald Campbell, the superintendent of Darjeeling, and collected rhododendrons unknown to European science. His book, The Rhododendrons of Sikkim-Himalaya, appeared from 1849 to 1851, and seeds he sent home started a craze for Himalayan rhododendrons in British gardens. We do not know that Hooker walked this exact ridge, so we claim only Sikkim.

Today the forest is protected as a sanctuary of about 104 km², with the Guras Kunj hut on the ridge as the only place to sleep inside it. Guras kunj loosely means rhododendron grove. Spring brings walkers from Siliguri, Kolkata and beyond, and most come for one short walk. Stay longer and you may also hear pheasants calling at dawn. Sikkim's state bird, the blood pheasant, lives in these high forests, though seeing one is never guaranteed.
story.source: Wikipedia: Varsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, Rhododendron arboreum, Blood pheasant, Archibald Campbell and Joseph Hooker; Hooker, The Rhododendrons of Sikkim-Himalaya (1849–51)

did_you_know: Varsey Rhododendron Sanctuary covers about 104 km² and borders Nepal to the west and West Bengal to the south across the Rambong Khola.
Rhododendron arboreum is the national flower of Nepal, while Sikkim's state tree is Rhododendron niveum.
The blood pheasant is the state bird of Sikkim.

highlights.title: The Hilley–Barsey walk
highlights.text: A wide, gently graded forest trail of about 4 km leads from the Hilley gate to the Barsey ridge in 1.5–2 hours. Most fit families and slow-walking seniors manage it. Start early for quiet trails, clear views and the best chance of birds.

highlights.title: Rhododendron bloom
highlights.text: Rhododendrons flower here from March to May. Near the ridge at about 3,000 m, the usual peak is mid-March to April, with reds first and paler shades later. A cold or dry winter can shift the dates, so ask in Okhrey before you go.

highlights.title: Guras Kunj at sunrise
highlights.text: The Guras Kunj trekkers' hut is the only lodging inside the sanctuary. It is simple, but a night here means sunset and sunrise on the ridge, with Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Pandim to the north on clear days, mostly October to December.

highlights.title: Birds of the high forest
highlights.text: Blood pheasant, Sikkim's state bird, satyr tragopan and Himalayan monal are all possible in these forests, along with Tibetan serin and laughingthrushes. Sightings are never guaranteed. Walk quietly at dawn and bring binoculars.

highlights.title: Three ways in
highlights.text: Hilley is the easy, popular entry. Dentam and Soreng are the other two gates, with longer, quieter forest routes that need a local guide and a full day. They suit walkers who want to avoid spring crowds.

highlights.title: A low-cost day out
highlights.text: With an Okhrey homestay, a shared car to Hilley and an entry fee of ₹50–100 for Indians, indicative, 2026, a Barsey day costs very little. The walk and the views are the whole point, and they are free.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri or Darjeeling to Jorethang, then a local jeep to Sombaria or Okhrey, about ₹150–250 a seat, indicative, 2026. From Okhrey, hire a car to Hilley, about 30 minutes, or ask your homestay to arrange one. Jeeps from Jorethang mostly leave before about 1 pm. Check current status before you travel.

A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra to Okhrey costs about ₹5,500–7,500 one way, 5–6 hours via Jorethang and Sombaria, then 30 minutes more to Hilley, indicative, 2026. From Okhrey, a local car to Hilley and back with waiting costs about ₹1,200–2,000.

New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and Bagdogra Airport (IXB), both in Siliguri, are the nearest railhead and airport. Plan a full day of road travel to Okhrey and walk the next morning. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit; check current status before you travel.

From the Hilley checkpost, walk about 4 km to Barsey, 1.5–2 hours up and a little less down. The trail is wide and clear. Longer routes enter from Dentam and Soreng and need a local guide and a full day.

where_to_stay: Inside the sanctuary, the only place to sleep is the Guras Kunj trekkers' hut on the Barsey ridge. It is basic: shared rooms or dormitory beds, simple meals, limited water and power, and cold nights. Book through your Okhrey homestay or operator and confirm it is open. Most people instead stay in Okhrey, about 30 minutes below Hilley, in Sherpa family homestays such as Sherpa Lodge, Kyilkhor Inn or Royal Barsey Homestay, at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day with meals, indicative, 2026. Rinchenpong and Uttarey also work as bases with a longer drive.
costs: ₹50–100 per person, more for foreigners and cameras, indicative, 2026
Local guide for Dentam or Soreng routes
budget_tip: Do Barsey as a day walk from an Okhrey homestay and share the Hilley car with other guests; the entry fee is then your only other cost.
tips: Start from Hilley by 7 am; cloud and haze usually build by late morning, especially in spring.
Carry water, snacks and a rain jacket, as there are few shops on the trail.
Wear shoes with grip, because the trail can be muddy and slippery after rain or snow.
Do not pick rhododendron flowers or leave litter; it is a protected sanctuary.
In January and February snow can cover the ridge, and from June to September the trail is wet and leech-filled; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Hilley to Barsey rhododendron walk
experiences.summary: Walk about 4 km from the Hilley gate to the Barsey ridge on a gentle forest trail, through rhododendron in bloom from March to May. It takes 1.5–2 hours each way and suits most fit families. Start early for clear skies.
body: The walk starts at Hilley, the road head and main entry gate of the sanctuary, about 30 minutes by car above Okhrey. Pay the entry fee at the checkpost, usually ₹50–100 per person for Indian nationals and more for foreigners and cameras, indicative, 2026. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel. Toilets and tea stalls near the gate are basic and may be shut early in the day.

From the gate a broad trail climbs gently for about 4 km to Barsey, 1.5–2 hours at an easy pace. It runs through forests of rhododendron, oak and magnolia, with moss and ferns on the trunks. In bloom season, mid-March to April near the top, the trees flower in reds, pinks and whites. Some years bloom comes early or late, so ask in Okhrey the evening before.

At the top, the forest opens onto the Barsey ridge and the Guras Kunj hut. On clear mornings you see Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Pandim to the north. In spring, haze often hides them by 10 am, which is why we start at dawn. Rest, take photos, and walk back the same way. Carry all rubbish out with you and leave the flowers on the trees.

faqs.q: Is the Barsey trek difficult
faqs.a: No. The Hilley to Barsey walk is about 4 km one way on a wide, gently graded forest trail, taking 1.5–2 hours up. Most reasonably fit adults, children of about eight and above, and seniors who walk slowly can manage it. It can be muddy after rain, so wear shoes with grip.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary
faqs.a: Entry is usually about ₹50–100 per person for Indian nationals, with higher fees for foreign nationals and extra charges for cameras, indicative, 2026. Pay at the Hilley checkpost and keep the receipt. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see rhododendrons at Barsey
faqs.a: Rhododendrons flower from March to May, and the usual peak near the Barsey ridge at about 3,000 m is mid-March to April. Exact timing depends on the winter's weather. For clear mountain views rather than flowers, October to December is better.

experiences.title: Night at Guras Kunj and Kangchenjunga sunrise
experiences.best_time: Oct–Dec for views; Mar–Apr for bloom
experiences.cost: Hut bed and meals extra; confirm rates locally
experiences.summary: Stay a night in the simple Guras Kunj trekkers' hut on the Barsey ridge. You get the forest to yourself after day walkers leave, a sunset over the Singalila Range and, on clear mornings, sunrise on Kangchenjunga. Book ahead and pack warm.
body: Guras Kunj is the trekkers' hut at the top of the Hilley trail and the only lodging inside the sanctuary. It is basic: shared rooms or dormitory beds, simple meals of rice, dal and vegetables, limited water and power, and no heating. What it offers is location. After the day walkers leave in the afternoon, the ridge goes quiet, and you may hear pheasants calling from the forest below.

On clear evenings the sun sets across the Singalila Range towards Nepal. Before dawn, step outside with a torch and a warm jacket and face north. Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m the world's third-highest mountain, catches the first light, with Kabru and Pandim beside it. October to December gives the best chance of a clear sunrise. In spring, the trade-off is flowers with more haze.

Book the hut through your Okhrey homestay or an operator and confirm it is open, because opening depends on season and management. Rates change, so ask when you book. Bring a sleeping bag liner or warm layers, a head torch, water purification, snacks and cash. Nights are cold all year and can fall below freezing from December to March. Walk out the next morning after breakfast.

faqs.q: Can you stay overnight at Barsey
faqs.a: Yes. The Guras Kunj trekkers' hut on the Barsey ridge is the only lodging inside the sanctuary. It is basic, with shared rooms or dorm beds and simple meals. Book through an Okhrey homestay or an operator and confirm it is open before you walk up.

faqs.q: Can you see Kangchenjunga from Barsey
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days you see Kangchenjunga, Kabru and Pandim to the north from the Barsey ridge. October to December gives the clearest mornings. In spring, haze often hides the peaks after early morning, and in the monsoon cloud usually covers them.

faqs.q: How cold is Guras Kunj at night
faqs.a: At about 3,000 m, Guras Kunj is cold at night all year. In spring expect close to freezing, and from December to February well below, with possible snow. There is no heating, so bring thermals, a down or heavy fleece jacket, a cap, gloves and warm socks.

experiences.title: Birding for pheasants in the high forest
experiences.summary: Walk the Barsey trails slowly at dawn with binoculars and a local guide. Blood pheasant, satyr tragopan and Himalayan monal are possible, along with Tibetan serin and laughingthrushes. Nothing is guaranteed, but early, quiet mornings give the best chance.
body: Barsey's high forests of rhododendron, oak and fir are good bird country. The blood pheasant, Sikkim's state bird, lives in these forests, and so do the satyr tragopan and the Himalayan monal, whose males are some of the most colourful birds in the Himalaya. All three are possible here, but they are shy, and a sighting is a lucky bonus, not a promise. Wikipedia also lists Tibetan serin and spotted laughingthrush for the sanctuary.

The best time is the first two hours of daylight. Start from Hilley at dawn, or step out from Guras Kunj before breakfast, and walk slowly and quietly. Pheasants often feed on the trail edges and in clearings, then melt into the undergrowth. Listen for calls before you look. Spring, from March to May, brings breeding calls and colour, and October to November brings clear mornings with fewer walkers.

A local guide who knows the calls and the usual spots makes a real difference; expect about ₹1,000–1,800 a day, indicative, 2026. Bring binoculars, wear dull colours and keep your voice low. Do not use playback calls to draw birds out, and never chase them off the trail. Stay on the path, take your litter back, and report anything unusual to the forest staff at Hilley.

faqs.q: Can I see the blood pheasant at Barsey
faqs.a: It is possible but not guaranteed. The blood pheasant, Sikkim's state bird, lives in the high forests around Barsey. Your best chance is a slow, quiet walk at dawn, ideally with a local guide who knows its calls. Spring and autumn mornings are best.

faqs.q: Which birds can I see in Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary
faqs.a: Possible birds include blood pheasant, satyr tragopan, Himalayan monal, Tibetan serin, spotted laughingthrush and other laughingthrushes, tits and finches of the high forest. Pheasants are shy and sightings are luck. Small forest birds are easier to see, especially at dawn.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for birding at Barsey
faqs.a: Not for the main trail, which is easy to follow, but a local guide who knows the calls greatly improves your chances. Expect about ₹1,000–1,800 a day, indicative, 2026. Ask your Okhrey homestay to arrange one, and agree the fee in advance.

experiences.title: Dentam and Soreng routes into Barsey
experiences.summary: Besides Hilley, the sanctuary has entry points at Dentam and Soreng. These longer forest routes are quieter and more demanding, need a full day and a local guide, and suit fit walkers who want Barsey without the spring crowds.
body: Varsey Rhododendron Sanctuary has three entry points: Hilley, Dentam and Soreng. Almost everyone uses Hilley, because the road reaches it and the walk is only 4 km. Dentam lies to the north, on the road between Pelling and Uttarey near Singshore Bridge, and Soreng to the east. Routes from these sides climb longer distances through forest and see far fewer walkers, even in April.

Because these trails are long, little used and not always marked, we do not give fixed distances or timings; they depend on the exact route and your pace. Plan a full day, start at first light and go with a local guide who knows the paths. Many walkers combine one of these routes with the Hilley trail, entering one way and leaving the other, with a car waiting at the far end.

Carry water, food, a rain jacket, a warm layer, a torch and a basic first-aid kit. Pay the sanctuary fee at the forest checkpost, and check current status before you travel, because paths can be damaged by landslides after the monsoon. These routes suit fit walkers in October to December or March to May. Avoid them from June to September and in snow.

faqs.q: What are the entry points for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary
faqs.a: There are three: Hilley, Dentam and Soreng. Hilley is the most popular, as it is reachable by road and Barsey is only about 4 km away on foot. Dentam and Soreng routes are longer forest walks that need a full day and a local guide.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Dentam to Barsey
faqs.a: Yes, Dentam is one of the sanctuary's entry points, but the route is much longer than the Hilley trail and less used. Go with a local guide, start at first light and plan a full day. Check path conditions after the monsoon and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory for Barsey
faqs.a: For the Hilley trail, a guide is not usually required, as the path is wide and clear. For the Dentam and Soreng routes we strongly suggest one, because paths split and are less used. Forest rules can change, so ask at the checkpost and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary
faqs.a: Barsey, officially Varsey, Rhododendron Sanctuary lies on the Singalila Range in the south-west of Sikkim, covering about 104 km². It borders Nepal to the west and West Bengal to the south across the Rambong Khola. The usual entry is Hilley, about 30 minutes by road above Okhrey village.

faqs.q: How do I reach Barsey from Siliguri
faqs.a: Travel from Siliguri or NJP to Okhrey via Jorethang and Sombaria, about 130 km and 5–6 hours. A reserved car costs about ₹5,500–7,500, or take shared jeeps via Jorethang, indicative, 2026. Sleep in Okhrey, drive 30 minutes to Hilley at dawn, then walk 4 km to Barsey.

faqs.q: How long is the Barsey trek
faqs.a: From Hilley the walk to Barsey is about 4 km one way, 1.5–2 hours up on a gentle forest trail, so the return trip takes 4–5 hours with rest stops. Longer routes start from Dentam and Soreng and take a full day with a guide.

faqs.q: Is Barsey good for children and seniors
faqs.a: Yes, for most. The Hilley trail is wide and gently graded, and children of about eight and up and seniors who walk slowly usually manage it. There are no ponies or vehicles on the trail, so anyone who cannot walk 8 km in a day should stay at Okhrey.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Barsey
faqs.a: Mid-March to April is best for rhododendron bloom near the ridge, with flowering from March to May overall. October to December is best for clear Kangchenjunga views. January and February may bring snow, and June to September brings rain, leeches and cloud, so avoid those months.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Barsey
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit, only the sanctuary entry ticket at Hilley and photo ID. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online or at Melli checkpost, and pay a higher entry fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there accommodation inside Barsey sanctuary
faqs.a: Only the Guras Kunj trekkers' hut on the Barsey ridge, which is basic, with shared rooms or dorm beds and simple meals. Most visitors sleep in Okhrey homestays, about 30 minutes below Hilley, and walk in and out in a day. Book Guras Kunj ahead and confirm it is open.

faqs.q: Can I see snow at Barsey
faqs.a: Sometimes. Snow can fall on the Barsey ridge, at about 3,000 m, from December to February, and occasionally in early March. It is not guaranteed and can make the trail slippery. Ask your Okhrey homestay about conditions, wear shoes with grip and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I pack for Barsey
faqs.a: Pack shoes with good grip, a warm jacket, a rain jacket, a cap, water, snacks, sunscreen and a torch. Add binoculars for birds and cash for fees and the car to Hilley. If staying at Guras Kunj, bring thermals, gloves and a sleeping bag liner, as nights are cold.
